callouts.label: Actin filament (F-actin)
callouts.hint: Two intertwined helical strands of light blue spherical monomers in the left panel — the thinnest of the three filament types.
callouts.description: Actin filaments (also called microfilaments or F-actin) are the thinnest cytoskeletal filaments at ~7 nm diameter. Each filament is a double helix of polymerized G-actin monomers. Actin filaments are concentrated just beneath the plasma membrane (cell cortex) where they maintain cell shape, enable cell crawling via lamellipodia and filopodia, and form the contractile ring during cytokinesis. In muscle cells, actin filaments interact with myosin to generate contractile force.
callouts.ap_tip: The college placement exam tests actin's role in THREE key processes: (1) cell motility via pseudopodia, (2) cytokinesis via the cleavage furrow contractile ring, and (3) muscle contraction via the sliding filament model with myosin. Know that actin is dynamic — it constantly polymerizes and depolymerizes (treadmilling).

callouts.label: G-actin monomer
callouts.hint: Individual spherical blue subunit within the actin double helix in the left panel.
callouts.description: G-actin (globular actin) is the monomeric subunit that polymerizes into F-actin filaments. Each G-actin monomer binds one molecule of ATP, which is hydrolyzed to ADP after incorporation into the filament. This ATP hydrolysis creates a structural difference between the two ends of the filament, driving the dynamic treadmilling behavior where monomers are added at the plus end and lost from the minus end.
callouts.ap_tip: G-actin uses ATP (not GTP) for polymerization — contrast this with tubulin, which uses GTP. The college placement exam may ask about the energy source for cytoskeletal dynamics. Both actin and tubulin exhibit dynamic instability/treadmilling, but they use different nucleotides.

callouts.label: Plus end (actin)
callouts.hint: The upper end of the actin filament in the left panel — the faster-growing end with a slightly open appearance.
callouts.description: The plus end (also called the barbed end) of an actin filament is where net monomer addition occurs. G-actin-ATP monomers bind preferentially to this end because the critical concentration for polymerization is lower here than at the minus end. In a crawling cell, the plus ends of actin filaments are oriented toward the leading edge of the cell, pushing the plasma membrane forward as they polymerize.
callouts.ap_tip: Actin polymerization at the plus end drives cell motility — this is how white blood cells chase bacteria (chemotaxis) and how cells migrate during wound healing and embryonic development. The college placement exam connects actin dynamics to cell crawling and immune response.

callouts.label: Minus end (actin)
callouts.hint: The lower end of the actin filament in the left panel — the slower-growing end with a compact appearance.
callouts.description: The minus end (also called the pointed end) of an actin filament is where net monomer loss occurs. Monomers at this end have hydrolyzed their ATP to ADP, weakening their binding affinity. The simultaneous addition at the plus end and loss at the minus end creates treadmilling — the filament appears to move through the cytoplasm while individual monomers cycle through it.
callouts.ap_tip: Treadmilling is a key concept for the college placement exam: the filament maintains a roughly constant length while individual subunits flow through it from plus to minus end. This dynamic turnover allows rapid reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton in response to signals — essential for cell motility and shape changes.

callouts.label: Actin cross-section
callouts.hint: Small circular cross-section view in the lower-left area showing the two-strand arrangement of the actin filament viewed end-on.
callouts.description: The cross-section of an actin filament reveals its thin profile (~7 nm diameter) — the narrowest of all three cytoskeletal filament types. The two intertwined strands are visible as a figure-eight or double-dot pattern. This small diameter allows actin filaments to form dense meshworks and bundles in the cell cortex, where they create a gel-like layer that supports the plasma membrane.
callouts.ap_tip: Size comparison is a favorite college placement exam topic: microfilaments (7 nm) < intermediate filaments (10 nm) < microtubules (25 nm). Remember 'MIM' — Micro smallest, Intermediate middle, Microtubules largest.

callouts.label: Microtubule
callouts.hint: Large hollow cylindrical tube in the center panel made of alternating orange and dark blue subunits — the thickest filament type.
callouts.description: Microtubules are hollow cylindrical polymers ~25 nm in diameter, composed of 13 protofilaments arranged in a ring. Each protofilament is a chain of alpha-tubulin/beta-tubulin heterodimers stacked end-to-end. Microtubules radiate from the centrosome (microtubule organizing center, MTOC) near the nucleus and extend toward the cell periphery. They serve as tracks for intracellular transport (via motor proteins), form the mitotic spindle during cell division, and are the structural core of cilia and flagella (9+2 arrangement).
callouts.ap_tip: Microtubules are tested heavily on the college placement exam in THREE contexts: (1) mitotic spindle — separating chromosomes during mitosis/meiosis, (2) intracellular transport — kinesin and dynein motor proteins, (3) cilia and flagella — the 9+2 microtubule arrangement. Colchicine disrupts microtubules and blocks mitosis — a classic exam example of how drugs target the cytoskeleton.

callouts.label: Alpha-tubulin
callouts.hint: Orange spherical subunit alternating with dark blue subunits along each protofilament in the center panel.
callouts.description: Alpha-tubulin is one half of the tubulin heterodimer that forms microtubule protofilaments. It binds GTP non-exchangeably (the GTP is trapped and never hydrolyzed at this site). Alpha-tubulin is exposed at the minus end of the microtubule. The alpha/beta heterodimer is the functional unit of microtubule assembly — individual alpha or beta subunits do not polymerize alone.
callouts.ap_tip: The college placement exam does not typically distinguish alpha from beta tubulin individually, but knowing that tubulin uses GTP (not ATP) and that the heterodimer is the assembly unit helps with FRQ answers comparing cytoskeletal components.

callouts.label: Beta-tubulin
callouts.hint: Dark blue spherical subunit alternating with orange subunits along each protofilament in the center panel.
callouts.description: Beta-tubulin is the other half of the tubulin heterodimer. It binds GTP exchangeably — after incorporation into the microtubule, this GTP is hydrolyzed to GDP. Beta-tubulin is exposed at the plus end of the microtubule. GTP hydrolysis at the beta-tubulin site drives dynamic instability: when GTP hydrolysis catches up to the growing tip (loss of the GTP cap), the microtubule rapidly depolymerizes (catastrophe).
callouts.ap_tip: Dynamic instability — rapid switching between growth and shrinkage — is how the mitotic spindle 'searches' for kinetochores during mitosis. Microtubules grow and shrink until they capture a chromosome. Taxol (paclitaxel) stabilizes microtubules and prevents depolymerization, blocking mitosis — it is used as a cancer chemotherapy drug.

callouts.label: Microtubule cross-section
callouts.hint: Circular cross-section in the lower center panel showing a ring of 13 protofilaments surrounding a hollow center.
callouts.description: The cross-section of a microtubule reveals its distinctive hollow ring of 13 protofilaments, with a clear central lumen. This hollow architecture gives microtubules high compressive strength (resistance to bending) despite being only 25 nm in diameter. The hollow core may also serve as a channel for small molecule transport. The 13-protofilament arrangement is nearly universal across eukaryotic species.
callouts.ap_tip: The hollow structure of microtubules contrasts with the solid intermediate filaments and thin actin filaments. In cilia and flagella, 9 outer doublet microtubules surround 2 central singlet microtubules (the 9+2 arrangement). Dynein arms between doublets generate the bending motion. The college placement exam tests the 9+2 structure.

callouts.label: Kinesin motor protein
callouts.hint: Small green two-headed walking figure on the microtubule surface near the top (plus end), carrying a cargo vesicle.
callouts.description: Kinesin is a motor protein that walks along microtubules toward the plus end (away from the centrosome, toward the cell periphery). It has two globular head domains that alternately bind and release the microtubule in a hand-over-hand stepping motion, powered by ATP hydrolysis. Kinesin transports vesicles, organelles, and mRNA from the cell body toward the cell surface — critical in neurons for anterograde axonal transport.
callouts.ap_tip: Kinesin = plus-end directed = toward cell periphery (anterograde transport). Think 'K for Kinesin, K for Kick out to the edge.' The college placement exam tests motor protein directionality. In neurons, kinesin carries vesicles from the soma down the axon to the synaptic terminal. Each step of kinesin is ~8 nm and consumes one ATP.

callouts.label: Dynein motor protein
callouts.hint: Purple two-headed walking figure on the microtubule surface near the bottom (minus end), walking in the opposite direction from kinesin.
callouts.description: Dynein is a motor protein that walks along microtubules toward the minus end (toward the centrosome, toward the cell center). Cytoplasmic dynein transports cargo inward — including endosomes, lysosomes, and signaling complexes. Axonemal dynein is a different form found in cilia and flagella, where it generates the sliding force between microtubule doublets that produces the characteristic bending motion.
callouts.ap_tip: Dynein = minus-end directed = toward cell center (retrograde transport). Think 'D for Dynein, D for Draw inward.' The college placement exam tests dynein in TWO contexts: (1) cytoplasmic dynein for retrograde transport in neurons and other cells, (2) axonemal dynein for ciliary/flagellar beating. Kartagener syndrome (primary ciliary dyskinesia) results from defective dynein.

callouts.label: Intermediate filament
callouts.hint: Thick rope-like twisted bundle of orange fibrous protein strands in the right panel — medium diameter between actin and microtubules.
callouts.description: Intermediate filaments (IFs) are rope-like polymers ~10 nm in diameter — between actin filaments (7 nm) and microtubules (25 nm). Unlike actin and microtubules, IFs are NOT polar (no plus/minus ends) and do NOT undergo dynamic treadmilling. They are the most mechanically durable cytoskeletal element, providing tensile strength to resist stretching and shearing forces. IFs anchor cells at desmosomes and hemidesmosomes.
callouts.ap_tip: Intermediate filaments are the 'structural steel' of the cytoskeleton — they resist mechanical stress. The college placement exam tests their role in desmosomes (cell-cell junctions) and their tissue-specific diversity. Unlike actin and microtubules, IFs are NOT disrupted by colchicine or cytochalasin — they are more chemically stable.

callouts.label: Coiled-coil dimer
callouts.hint: Two darker orange alpha-helical protein chains wound around each other, visible where the rope unravels at the top of the right panel.
callouts.description: The basic building block of intermediate filaments is a coiled-coil dimer: two alpha-helical polypeptide chains wound around each other in a left-handed supercoil. Two dimers associate in an antiparallel, staggered fashion to form a tetramer — this antiparallel arrangement is why intermediate filaments have no overall polarity. Eight tetramers then wind together to form the final ~10 nm filament.
callouts.ap_tip: The antiparallel tetramer structure explains why intermediate filaments have no polarity and no motor proteins walk along them (motor proteins require directional tracks). This structural difference from actin and microtubules is a common college placement exam comparison point.

callouts.label: IF cross-section
callouts.hint: Circular cross-section in the lower-right area showing the dense, solid core of the intermediate filament — no hollow lumen.
callouts.description: The cross-section of an intermediate filament reveals a dense, solid core — in stark contrast to the hollow microtubule. The ~10 nm diameter reflects the tight packing of 32 polypeptide chains (8 tetramers × 4 chains). This solid construction gives intermediate filaments exceptional tensile strength, similar to a woven rope. The lack of a lumen means IFs cannot serve as transport tracks.
callouts.ap_tip: Solid core (IFs) vs. hollow tube (microtubules) is a key structural comparison on the college placement exam. The solid core makes IFs stronger under tension but unable to support motor protein transport. The hollow microtubule is weaker under compression but provides tracks for kinesin and dynein.

callouts.label: Keratin filaments
callouts.hint: Cluster of light orange intermediate filaments at the bottom-right, representing the dense network found in epithelial cells.
callouts.description: Keratin is the most common type of intermediate filament protein, found in epithelial cells. Keratin filaments form a dense intracellular network that connects to desmosomes (cell-cell junctions) and hemidesmosomes (cell-matrix junctions), distributing mechanical stress across the tissue. Different keratin subtypes are expressed in different epithelia — hard keratins in hair and nails, soft keratins in skin. Lamins (nuclear IFs) and neurofilaments (neuronal IFs) are other tissue-specific examples.
callouts.ap_tip: The college placement exam tests tissue-specific IF proteins: keratin in epithelial cells, lamins in the nuclear lamina (all cells), vimentin in mesenchymal cells, neurofilaments in neurons, desmin in muscle cells. Epidermolysis bullosa simplex results from mutant keratin genes — skin blisters easily because cells cannot resist mechanical stress.
